blocks.x: This tab answers: what the player feels from first launch to hundredth hour, and what the interface and sound do to protect that feeling.
Start with 4.1 and 4.3; they expose missing screens before art begins. Treat 4.7 as a shipping requirement, not a polish pass.
Write the journey from the player's clock, not the feature list. Name what they do, what they feel, and what could break the session at each stage.

In the first five minutes B.E.E.P. wakes in the cargo lander, moves one crate before the air timer hits zero, and opens the airlock at 1:20. The first session ends at Shift 2 with air at 40 percent and a radio signal nobody can identify; the first failure, a dry garden, is recoverable next shift.

The first five minutes answer three questions without a menu: where am I, what can I do, and why care. Put the first action inside {{30 seconds}} and first success inside {{90 seconds}}. If the player watches more than plays, the opening is a trailer.
Opening: {{wake in the cargo lander and move one crate before air runs out}} · First success: {{the door opens}} · First surprise: {{the crew speaks to B.E.E.P. as if it cannot hear}}

A first session is a complete emotional unit, not a tutorial plus a game. End on a decision the player wants to return to, and make the save state legible: {{the next shift begins with air at 40 percent}}. Target {{20–40 minutes}} and test where players stop.
Length: {{25 minutes}} · Exit hook: {{the radio picks up a signal nobody can identify}} · Save prompt: {{autosave at the shift break with a one-line recap}}

The first week is about mastery and return. By session three the player has a routine, a chosen goal, and one system they understand better than the game explained. Track return after the first fail, not only the first win.
Session 3 goal: {{stabilize air for two shifts without resupply}} · Mastery moment: {{reroute a pipe without the hint}} · Return hook: {{a crew member asks a personal favour}}

Write the intended feeling as a curve with five points: {{curiosity, competence, attachment, doubt, resolve}}. Name the beat that produces each turn. If two adjacent beats produce the same feeling, one is padding.

The arc must survive failure. A player who loses a shift should feel {{determined}}, not {{stupid}}. If failure produces the second feeling, the feedback blames the player for a system the game did not teach.

blocks.x: Write five principles that can reject a design. 'Be intuitive' cannot reject anything; 'one decision per screen' can.

The HUD shows three numbers only: air, power, and shift time. When B.E.E.P. nears the air regulator, the world shows a teal gauge and an amber valve; the objective list stays one input away, so the player never reads a dashboard while the air runs out.

x: **One decision per screen.** Split destination, difficulty, and save-slot choices into separate screens.
**Show state before asking for input.** The player sees the relevant resources and timers before spending them.
**The world is the first menu.** Prefer a switch, door, or console over a list when the choice has a physical place.
**Every failure is visible before it is expensive.** Warn at the threshold, not after the loss.
**Two inputs to anywhere.** Any regular screen is reachable in two actions from gameplay.

blocks.x: Take a stance per system, not for the whole game. Resources can live in the world as gauges and tanks; objectives usually need a list because the world cannot narrate priority. Write the rule the UI team can apply without asking.
Diegetic: {{air, power, cargo, door locks}} · Non-diegetic: {{objectives, subtitles, settings}} · Hybrid: {{map, crew mood}}
Set a number for simultaneous information and test against it. A player tracking six resources is not managing a base; they are reading a dashboard.
Max HUD resources: {{3}} · Max active objectives: {{3}} · Max new terms per tutorial beat: {{1}} · Max choices per prompt: {{4}}

x: PC: hover reveals, right-click cancels, Esc pauses, and every action has a keyboard equivalent.
Console: face button confirms, B or Circle backs, triggers switch tabs, and focus never leaves the screen.
Handheld: text scales for a {{7-inch}} screen and touch targets are at least {{44 by 44 pixels}}.
Use platform controller glyphs and respect suspend and resume behaviour on every storefront.

blocks.x: Inventory screens before wireframing. Every screen needs an owner, one entry, and a defined back target; orphan screens become bugs.

The pause screen opens over a frozen frame and offers Resume, Objectives, Map, Settings, Save, and Quit. Back from Settings returns to the pause screen, back from Save shows the slot list, and Esc never quits to title without a confirmation.

x: Every screen has one primary action and one clear way back. Two competing back buttons are a coin flip.
Tabs remember their last position within a session; resetting to the first tab punishes exploration.
The pause menu opens over a frozen frame of gameplay, not a black screen; the player keeps their place.

x: Transitions under {{one second}} are cuts; over {{three seconds}} need a progress indicator and a tip.
Never show a spinner without a label; the player must know whether the game is saving, loading, or matching.
Use one transition language: {{fade to white for shift changes, fade to black for failure}}.

blocks.x: Draw the flow as boxes and arrows with one entry and one exit per screen. Label every arrow with the input that causes it. Keep the diagram in the repository and date it; a slide-deck copy is already stale.
Add a HUD element only after naming the decision it supports. If the player never acts on it, move it to a menu or remove it.

The air meter sits top left, stays visible in every shift, and turns red at 20 percent with a pulsing icon and a low hiss. It hides only in menus and cutscenes; the power meter sits beneath it and fades when the workshop is off.
Set minimum sizes in pixels, not points. Test on a TV at {{three metres}} and a handheld at {{30 centimetres}}. If the player leans in, the HUD is too small.
Minimum body text: {{24 px}} · Minimum HUD label: {{18 px}} · Minimum contrast: {{4.5:1}} · Maximum HUD text lines: {{2}}
Keep critical UI inside the title-safe area. TVs overscan and some monitors crop edges; a timer at the edge is a timer the player cannot see.
Safe margin: {{5 percent of screen width}} · TV-safe: {{10 percent}} · Subtitle baseline: {{12 percent above the bottom edge}}

x: Use two channels for every critical state: colour plus icon, sound plus screen edge, motion plus text.
Show direction before magnitude; the player needs to know where the problem is before how bad it is.
Fade feedback once the cause is resolved; a permanent red icon teaches the player to ignore red.
Remove the element. Can the player still make the decision it supported?
If yes, leave it removed.
If no, can the world show it instead of the HUD? If yes, move it and retest.
If no, keep it and write the reason in the HUD table.

blocks.x: Design the menu tree as a flat list of destinations first. Group by player intent, not by internal system name.

Defaults ship subtitles on, shake reduced, and hold-to-toggle off. The game autosaves at each shift start and before the garden vote, keeps three rotating autosaves plus ten manual slots, and shows a cloud-conflict card with both timestamps before the player chooses.
Write the tree as indented text, then count the depth. The player should never be more than three choices from quitting, saving, or turning on subtitles.

Title: {{Continue · New Shift · Settings · Credits · Quit}} · Pause: {{Resume · Objectives · Map · Settings · Save · Quit}} · Settings: {{Display · Audio · Controls · Accessibility · Gameplay · Language}}
Defaults are the design. Most players never open settings, so ship the most accessible version: subtitles on, shake reduced, toggle instead of hold, and a difficulty that forgives a first mistake.

x: Confirm destructive actions only: overwrite save, quit with unsaved progress, delete a base, spend premium currency.
Do not confirm reversible actions; a prompt on every repair trains the player to mash through.
Put the consequence in the button label: {{Overwrite save 2}}, not {{OK}}.

blocks.x: Teach one verb per beat, test it immediately, then reinforce it in a new context. If a tutorial needs a wall of text, the interaction is not ready.

The first run opens on B.E.E.P. in the lander with one prompt: 'Hold E to lift the crate.' The air timer starts at 60 seconds; opening the airlock at 1:20 completes the teach-test beat. The repair verb returns on Shift 3 at the frozen garden pipe, ten minutes after the first lesson.

**Teach, test, reinforce.** Teach with a prompt and demonstration, test with a task the player cannot complete by accident, and reinforce by requiring the verb again {{ten minutes later}}. A verb taught once is a cutscene with a button.

x: Show the title and one action: {{Continue or New Shift}}.
Load into a playable moment; no logo chain longer than {{eight seconds}}.
Teach movement and one interaction in the first {{30 seconds}}.
Give the first success before the first failure.
Ask about accessibility once, with sensible defaults and a skip.
Show a prompt when the player is near the relevant object and has not used it yet; hide it after the first success.
Use the verb in the prompt: {{Hold E to repair}}, not {{Interact}}.
One prompt at a time; stacked prompts hide the world and make the player read instead of look.
Every tutorial beat is skippable from the pause menu and replayable from the help screen.
Skipping sets the same flags as completing; the player must not be locked out of a mechanic.
Offer a practice room for timing verbs; do not gate story progress on a timing test.

blocks.x: Set the accessibility target before content lock. Retrofitting subtitles, remapping, and scalable text costs three to five times more than building them in.

Subtitles ship on by default with speaker names and bracketed sounds such as [air hiss] and [lock click]. Text scales to 200 percent, the HUD passes 4.5:1 contrast, and every action is remappable; the air alarm also flashes the screen edge and shows a red icon, never colour alone.

Accessibility is a set of shipping requirements with owners and test cases, not a values statement. Name the standard, the options, and the person who signs off. Test with assistive technology and with players, not only with a checklist.

blocks.label: Non-negotiable
blocks.x: The player should never lose because the UI failed to communicate. Treat unreadable text, missing subtitles, and ambiguous status as gameplay bugs with the same severity as a crash.

Target WCAG 2.2 AA for menus and text, the Xbox Accessibility Guidelines for console input and display, and PlayStation requirements for system features. Certification is the floor, not the goal; record the guideline version in the plan.

x: Minimum {{24 px}} body text at 1080p; support {{200 percent}} UI scaling without clipping.
Contrast at least {{4.5:1}} for body text and {{3:1}} for large text and icons.
Never use colour alone; pair every state with an icon, shape, or label.
Offer reduced motion, reduced flash, and a camera-shake slider.
Subtitles on by default, with speaker names for off-screen lines and bracketed sound descriptions.
Show a visual cue for every sound that carries gameplay information: {{alarm, air leak, door lock}}.
Provide mono audio and separate volume sliders for voice, music, SFX, and UI.
Every action is remappable; no action requires two buttons held for more than {{three seconds}}.
No quick-time event requires more than {{two presses per second}}; offer a hold alternative.
Touch targets are at least {{44 by 44 pixels}} with {{8 pixels}} spacing.
Pause anywhere, including cutscenes, with a readable recap on return.
Keep three visible objectives and restate the current one in the pause menu.
Offer a story recap and controls card after an absence longer than {{seven days}}.

blocks.x: Do not require speech input. If voice commands exist, provide a full controller or keyboard equivalent and never make voice the only path. Caption all voiced content, including warning barks.
**Accessibility commitment:** 'Every screen ships readable, remappable, and captioned. If a player cannot see the state, hear the cue, or reach the button, the screen is not done.'
Describe sound as behaviour: what triggers it, what it tells the player, and what it must never mask. Loudness and budget belong here, not in a separate document nobody opens.

The base bed runs at 82 BPM with felt piano, muted strings, and a soft pad. When air drops below 30 percent, a ticking string layer enters and the pad ducks 6 dB under Imani's radio line; restoring the air unit fades the tension layer over eight seconds.

Name the instrumentation, tempo range, and emotional job. A cosy base builder needs {{warm acoustic timbres, a slow pulse, and silence that feels safe rather than empty}}. Write two references and one anti-reference to stop generic epic.
Instrumentation: {{felt piano, muted strings, soft analog pad, small percussion}} · Tempo: {{70–100 BPM}} · Anti-reference: {{trailer drums and heroic brass}}
State recorded minutes, speaker count, and languages, then state what is text-only. A barks-only character can carry personality for a fraction of a full VO budget.
VO: {{2,500 lines, 110 minutes, 8 speakers, 5 languages}} · Text-only: {{lore, item descriptions, codex}} · Barks: {{600 lines, no lip-sync}}

x: Dialogue and critical alerts, always audible.
Player action feedback: repair, pickup, damage.
Objective and navigation cues.
Music, ducked under dialogue by {{6 dB}}.

blocks.x: Set the budget in megabytes, streams, and simultaneous voices. Then set the cut rule: {{ambience variants before dialogue, dialogue before critical alerts}}.
Budget: {{450 MB}} · Streams: {{2 music, 1 ambience}} · Voices: {{24 simultaneous}} · Compression: {{Vorbis for SFX, ADPCM for short UI}}

Choose middleware before the first sound is integrated. FMOD and Wwise both work; the choice matters less than event naming, the parameter list, and who owns the bank build. Put the version in the build notes.
Write for translation from the first string. Keep sentences short, avoid variables in the middle of grammar, and never build a sentence by concatenating fragments.

Tier 1 ships English, French, German, Spanish, and Portuguese with full text and VO; German buttons run 30 percent longer, so the save menu reserves two lines. The subtitle event 'Imani: The resupply is late.' runs 1.8 seconds at 18 characters per second, inside the 42-character line limit.
Count strings and words by surface, then add a growth margin. UI labels grow faster than dialogue because there is no room to wrap.
Strings: {{8,500}} · Words: {{95,000}} · Growth margin: {{20 percent}} · Longest UI label: {{24 characters}}

x: Use a family with Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, and CJK coverage, or a tested fallback chain.
Test every glyph before localization lock; a missing glyph is a blank button.
Never bake text into textures or 3D assets; localize it as a string with a layout slot.
Review icons, gestures, holidays, and colour meanings per region; a thumbs-up is not universal.
Check names and number formats against target locales; dates and currency are part of the text.
Flag idioms, sarcasm, and wordplay for adaptation, not literal translation.

blocks.x: Decide whether localized VO is dubbing or subtitles only, and budget it. Dubbing needs lip-sync retiming, a local casting director, and a second QA pass. If only original VO ships, say so on the store page and language screen.

x: Minimum {{one second}}, maximum {{seven seconds}} per subtitle event.
Maximum {{two lines}} and {{42 characters per line}} for Latin scripts; use per-language limits.
Reading speed {{15–20 characters per second}} for adults; lower for younger audiences.
Never split a sentence across a cutscene cut; re-time the line instead.

blocks.x: Do not call the experience finished until a new player can complete the first session, a returning player can resume, and an accessibility tester can use every screen.
